phonemes.desc: Aspirated theta [tʰ], the breathy initial consonant.
Long eta [ɛː], the first syllable's length.
Short iota with acute plus alpha — the pitch peak on the second syllable.

pronunciation.approximation: 'thay-EE-ah' — the first syllable is long and level, the second pitched high and bright.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Θεία (Theía), Titaness of sight, shining, and the bright upper air

kin.label: Root
kin.form: θέα (théa), 'sight, view'; related to θεάομαι, 'to gaze'

kin.label: Children
kin.form: Hēlios, Selēnē, and Eōs — sun, moon, and dawn

pronunciation.note: Theía is Tier 1 because the Greek Θεία contains both length (η in the first syllable) and stress (acute on the ι of the second). She is the Titaness whose children are the celestial lights.

domains.title: Titaness of Sight and Light
domains.subtitle: Brilliance, The Eyes, The Celestial Luminaries
domains.lead: Theía is the Titaness of sight, shining, and the bright ether. Though less famous than her children Hēlios, Selḗnē, and Ēōs, she is the luminous source from which they spring — the divine principle that makes seeing and being seen possible. Hesiod gives her one marriage and three children; Pindar gives her a golden hymn; the rest is inference.

cards.name: Mother of Lights
cards.desc: By Hyperion she bore the sun, moon, and dawn — every light that crosses the sky (Theogony 371–374).

cards.name: Goddess of Sight
cards.desc: Her name belongs to the root θέα, 'sight'; she is the shining by which anything is seen at all.

cards.name: Shining Ether
cards.desc: She personifies the bright upper air through which light travels to the eye — the medium, not the lamp.

cards.name: Titanic Lineage
cards.desc: Daughter of Ouranos and Gaia, sister of Kronos and Rhea, aunt of Zeus — born with the first generation.

symbols.name: The gold crown
symbols.meaning: Her Hesiodic attribute — 'Theía, crowned with gold' (Theogony 135) — radiance worn as royalty.

symbols.name: Radiant eyes
symbols.meaning: The organs of sight, her namesake province; she is the light by which seeing happens.

symbols.name: Sun, moon, and dawn
symbols.meaning: Her three children — the visible proof of her marriage to Hyperion, and her true portrait.

symbols.name: The bright ether
symbols.meaning: The luminous upper air she personifies, through which every ray descends to the world.

symbols.name: Flash on gold and water
symbols.meaning: Pindar's image (Isthmian 5): her radiance glimpsed on metal and on the sea — the sun's distant gleam that sailors read.

mythology.lead: Theía has no independent narrative myths; her importance is genealogical and cosmological. Through her, the Titans bequeath light to the Olympian cosmos — and the tradition is honest enough to leave her otherwise silent. Two lines of Hesiod, an ode of Pindar, and a name that became a science are her whole surviving estate.

myths.title: Birth of the Luminaries
myths.text: Hesiod mentions Theía exactly where her meaning lives. First, in the Titan catalogue, she is simply 'Theía, crowned with gold' (Theogony 135) — one word of ornament, and the only one he ever gives her. Then, at 371–374: 'Hyperion lay in love with Theía of the gold crown, and she bore him great Hēlios and bright Selḗnē and Ēōs, who brings light to all mortals and to the deathless gods.' That is the entirety of her recorded mythology — a birth, a marriage, three children — and it is enough to found a cosmology: the upper air wed to the high one, and every light that crosses the sky as their offspring. Later Greek poets repeat the triad without ever adding a scene; the goddess's silence in the tradition may itself be the myth — the medium of light does not appear; it makes appearing possible.

myths.title: Pindar's Theia of Many Names
myths.text: Pindar opens Isthmian 5 with the most vivid address Theía ever received: 'Mother of the Sun, Theia of many names' — and immediately explains the 'many names': it is because of her that mortals count gold as the most powerful of things, for the radiance of her doings shows upon gold and its gleam. The ancient scholiasts add the practical detail: sailors at sea see Theía in the sun's distant flash on the waves, reading the horizon by her. The logic is antique and precise — the goddess of the shining ether is present wherever light becomes visible as radiance: on metal, on water, on the glint that betrays a ship over the horizon. Her epithet also hints at a theological elasticity: the same luminous principle answers to whatever the moment requires — sight, splendor, the flash of gold. Theía is not a character but an optics, and Pindar hymns her as such.

myths.title: Sight, Wonder, and the Divine
myths.text: Ancient and modern scholars alike connect Theía's name with θέα, 'sight', and the verb θεάομαι, 'to gaze in wonder' — the same root family as θέατρον, 'theater', and θεωρία, 'contemplation'. Later Greek writers could not resist the further step: that θεά, 'goddess', belongs to the same family — the divine as that which shines forth and is seen. The second derivation is linguistically shaky, and a scholarly entry must say so plainly; but the intuition was deeply Greek, and Plato's vocabulary of the knowable as 'visible in its radiance' lives in the same semantic field. Her gold crown completes the picture: the goddess of sight wears the substance that most resembles what sight loves. If her cult was negligible, her word-family conquered the language — theory, theater, and theology are all, etymologically, her daughters too.

myths.title: Among the Fallen Titans
myths.text: Hesiod does not show Theía fighting in the Titanomachy, but the arithmetic of Theogony 717–720 leaves her no exemption: after the ten-year war, Zeus's side bound the Titans and hurled them 'into murky Tartarus, as far beneath the earth as earth is beneath heaven'. The Titanesses as a group disappear from the poem into that fall — while their luminous children ride on overhead, untouchable. Theía's fate, if she shared it, is the cosmic version of her own nature: the ether cannot be imprisoned, but the personification can. Later tradition quietly released her: she survives in Pindar and in the scholia as the ever-present mother of light, unshrined by any city but unexcluded from any sky — a goddess whose temple is whatever the light touches, and whose only liturgy is the daybreak itself.

lore.syncretism: Rome produced no Theía — Latin mythographers list her among the Titans (Hyginus, Fabulae praefatio), but no Roman cult developed and no Roman equivalent was invented; her name crossed into Latin only as a learned genealogy. In later antique thought her province was absorbed by the radiance-cults around Sol and by Neoplatonic meditations on light as the first emanation. Her most striking reception is modern: planetary scientists named the Mars-sized protoplanet of the giant-impact hypothesis — the body whose collision with the infant Earth threw up the debris that became the Moon — 'Theia'. It is a strangely perfect tribute: the Titaness of shining, invoked at the birth of the very moon her mythology first explained.
lore.culturalLegacy: Theía's afterlife is linguistic and scientific rather than cultic. From her root-family come theory, theater, and theorem — the Greek conviction that to see is to know, and that the highest knowing is a kind of beholding. Her children gave her a permanent gallery: every classical depiction of Hēlios rising, Selḗnē veiled, or Ēōs in her saffron robe is, indirectly, her portrait. In the twenty-first century her name passed permanently into the scientific lexicon through the Theia impact hypothesis — one of the few Titanesses whose name now appears in planetary-science textbooks. Restoring Theía restores the name of the brightness that makes brightness possible: the light before the lamp.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Theía is the unseen source of all that is seen. She has no myths because her power is too basic for narrative: it is the condition under which any story can be witnessed. To honor her is to recognize that light is not merely physical but epistemic — we know by seeing, and we are known by being seen.

Her restoration in Unicode is fitting. The very act of reading a restored Greek name on a screen depends on light, on sight, on luminous technology that her children prefigured. Theía reminds us that behind every visible marvel there is an older, quieter power: the brightness that makes brightness possible. The Greeks rarely prayed to her; they simply saw everything by her — which may be the purest form of worship there is.
lore.archaeology: No sanctuary of Theía is securely attested — Pausanias, who tours hundreds of shrines across Greece, offers her not one — and no independent image of her survives. She is visible only indirectly: in the countless representations of her children, Hēlios rising in his chariot, Selḗnē with billowing veil, Ēōs ascending in saffron, whose very ubiquity is her monument. Her name is fixed for us instead by the earliest Greek poetry — the two lines of Hesiod and the opening of Pindar's fifth Isthmian — a reminder that some gods are monuments of language rather than stone.
